sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Complete the sentence: The ____ grants ____ to the political parties and the candidates who contest elections.
questions.answer: Election Commission; election symbols

questions.q: True or False: (a) The Rashtriya Janata Dal was formed by Lalu Prasad Yadav in 1997. (b) The Shiv Sena is a political party of Tamil Nadu.
questions.answer: (a) True (b) False — it is a party of Maharashtra.

questions.q: True or False: (a) Regional political parties have emerged to fulfil regional aspirations. (b) At present India has a two-party system.
questions.answer: (a) True (b) False — India has a multi-party system.

questions.q: Answer in one word: (I) The Rashtriya Janata Dal is primarily a regional party of which state? (II) The All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam is primarily a regional party of which state?
questions.answer: (I) Bihar (II) Tamil Nadu

questions.q: Name the group as per the definitions: (1) An organised group of people which seeks to promote its specific interests. (2) A group which exerts influence/pressure in a strong, determined way to produce a particular result.
questions.answer: (1) Interest group (2) Pressure group

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The ____ led by the BJP and the ____ led by the Congress are the two main coalitions at the national level.
questions.answer: National Democratic Alliance (NDA); United Progressive Alliance (UPA)

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why does a political party aim to achieve power? Explain.
questions.answer: A party is formed by people with common principles and programmes. Only by winning elections and forming the government can it convert its manifesto into laws and policies and serve the people as promised; power is the means to implement its programme.

or.q: Why is the Indian party system called a multi-party system? Explain.
or.answer: Many national, State and registered parties compete for power; no single party usually wins a majority, so national parties depend on regional parties and form coalition governments (NDA, UPA). Hence it is a multi-party system, not one- or two-party.

questions.q: Explain any two major objectives of the Bharatiya Janata Party.
questions.answer: (1) Nationalism and national integration with democracy. (2) Positive secularism, Gandhian socialism and value-based politics.

questions.q: Explain two characteristics of a political party.
questions.answer: (1) It is an organised group of people sharing common principles and goals. (2) It seeks political power through peaceful, constitutional methods — elections — and puts its programme into practice when in power.

questions.q: Mention the conditions required to be recognised as a national political party.
questions.answer: According to the Election Commission (as given in the textbook): (1) it should be a recognised party in four or more States; (2) it should win a minimum share of seats (about 4% of Lok Sabha seats or 3.33% of assembly seats) and its candidates should poll at least 6% of valid votes.

questions.q: How do political parties help in running democratic processes?
questions.answer: They nominate candidates and contest elections, offer policy choices through manifestos, form the government or a responsible opposition, educate voters and shape public opinion, and link people with the government — without them elections and representative government would hardly be possible.

questions.q: Why are Civil Society Organisations considered a new form of mass pressure tactics? Two points.
questions.answer: (1) They are formed by ordinary committed citizens on issues like corruption, environment and women's rights and mobilise large numbers of people through peaceful methods. (2) They pressure the government to change policies and point out unfulfilled promises — e.g. MKSS's movement led to the RTI Act.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain any three challenges faced by political parties in India.
questions.answer: (1) Lack of internal democracy and dynastic succession — power stays with a few leaders and families. (2) Growing role of money and muscle power and criminalisation of politics. (3) Coalition compulsions and frequent switching of alliances make parties focus on short-term gains and emotive issues rather than ideology and lasting policies.

questions.q: Explain, with examples, the role of pressure groups.
questions.answer: (1) They promote, debate and mobilise public opinion on issues and educate people — e.g. trade unions like AITUC. (2) They press the government through petitions, lobbying, demonstrations, satyagraha and strikes — e.g. FICCI on industrial policy, Kisan Sabhas on farm prices. (3) They bring changes in policy — SEWA improved rules for women workers and MKSS secured the Right to Information law.

questions.q: Differentiate between national and regional political parties with examples.
questions.answer: (1) National parties have influence across the country and are recognised in four or more States — e.g. Congress, BJP, CPI(M), BSP. (2) Regional parties are strong in one or a few States and arise from regional aspirations — e.g. Shiv Sena (Maharashtra), DMK and AIADMK (Tamil Nadu), Trinamool Congress (West Bengal). (3) National parties take up national and international issues, while regional parties focus on their State's interests and often support coalitions at the Centre.

questions.q: How are pressure groups different from political parties? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Pressure groups are not primarily political and do not seek power directly; parties seek to form the government. (2) Pressure groups do not contest elections; parties nominate candidates and campaign. (3) Pressure groups have specific, limited interests and may have no ideology; parties have ideologies and broad national programmes.

questions.q: Differentiate between pressure groups and interest groups.
questions.answer: (1) An interest group is an organised group promoting specific interests of its members; a pressure group is an interest group that actively pressures the government. (2) Interest groups may or may not influence government policy; pressure groups must do so. (3) Interest groups are softer and more protective; pressure groups are strictly structured, harsher and both protective and promotive. All pressure groups are interest groups, but not all interest groups are pressure groups.

questions.q: Explain the importance of regional political parties in India.
questions.answer: (1) They fulfil regional aspirations and represent local issues, culture and language. (2) They often rule their States and play a vital role in forming coalition governments at the Centre, winning resources for their States. (3) They have federalised the party system and strengthened cooperative federalism.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain any six functions of political parties in India.
questions.answer: (1) They nominate candidates for elections. (2) They campaign to win support for their candidates. (3) They place their policies before voters through manifestos. (4) The party or coalition with a majority forms the government and makes and implements policies. (5) Parties in minority form the opposition, criticise and check the government. (6) They educate people, shape public opinion, articulate people's demands and act as a link between the people and the government.

or.q: What are Civil Society Organisations? Write the names of any four contemporary Civil Society Organisations in India.
or.answer: CSOs are associations, groups and voluntary agencies formed by citizens to pursue issues of common concern — environment, corruption, price rise, gender justice, child labour — acting as an interface between the State and the individual and pressing the government to change policies. Examples: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (Aruna Roy), Self-Employed Women's Association (Ela Bhatt), Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar), India Against Corruption (Anna Hazare); also PUCL and NAPM.

questions.q: Suggest any six effective measures to reform political parties.
questions.answer: (1) Ensure internal democracy — regular organisational elections within parties. (2) Make party finances transparent and audit them; limit election expenses. (3) Keep candidates with criminal records out of elections. (4) Enforce the anti-defection law to stop party-switching for gain. (5) Give fair representation to women and weaker sections in tickets and posts. (6) Encourage parties to campaign on policies and programmes rather than caste, religion and emotive slogans, and let citizens and the media keep a check.
